Fadó fadó, i n-áit darḃ ainm Taṁnaċ Ṁullaiġ, eadar Loċ Iasg agus an Bearnas Mór, ḃí sean-lánúin ina gcoṁnuiḋe i dtoiġ ḃeag ḟionn-aolta. Peadar agus Bríd Ṁic Ḟionntaiġ atá orṫu, agus óna dtoiġ ḃeag i mbaile fearainn Ġuala Duḃ, ṫig leat na Cruaċa Gorma agus trasna an loċa a ḟeiceáilt. Tráṫnóna saṁraiḋ aṁáin, faoi lán-ġealaiġ, ḃí Peadar ag teaċt aḃaile i ndiaiḋ ċuidiú le coṁarsa, agus ċonaic sé rud aisteaċ ina ċuiḃreann préataí féin! Ḃí planda aṁáin ina ċaor ċoiṁṫíoċ! D’aṁarc sé níos gaire ar an ṗlanda, agus d’aimsiġ sé foinse an tsolais. Ḃí mion-ġirseaċ ṁaiseaċ ina suiḋe ar ḋuilleog préata ann! Ní raḃ fad ordóige inti, agus ḃí solas suaiṁneaċ ag teaċt uaiṫi. Duḃairt Peadar leis an ṁion-ġirseaċ “Tá tú faiġte agam mar tá tú anseo, sna préataí a mbím ag siúḃail ṫairis gaċ lá. posts.title: LASID exploration: Gaelic words for "also"
posts.description: Digitising a valuable resource For a good few months, I have been working on and off on digitising Wagner's Linguistic Atlas and Survey of Irish Dialects, which comprises phonetic records collected in the 1950s and 60s. You can read more about the previous digitisation work by others that I am grateful to be building upon, my specific contributions, and the goals of my work at the Codeberg project . It will take a while for my vision for the LASID digitisation project to be fully realised, but in the meantime I thought it would be fun to publish some short blog posts on various dialectal observations and analyses, aided by my digitisation work. Map 85: also Map 85 in Volume 1 of the LASID shows the word used for "also" at the various survey points. The elicitation prompt was "your shirt is dirty too", with the prior prompt being "my shirt is dirty". Lexical observations From the plots above, we can see that leis is ubiquitous in Kerry and Cork. posts.title: Lucky piglets and little hatreds: on Gaelic terms for hedgehog
posts.description: Following on from frogject , I am continuing the theme of researching the creatures that live in my garden. This time, the humble hedgehog has his moment in the spotlight. A hogject , if you will. A recent visitor to my garden Gráinneog nó gràineag: not so hateful after all? Near-ubiquitous in the returns for the Linguistic Atlas and Survey of Irish Dialects (LASID) is the word gráinneog . Only two returns in Ireland offer alternative names, which we will address later. Of the seven Scottish survey points, only two give a name for the hedgehog, both variants of this word. The Digital Archive of Scottish Gaelic records usages in Argyll, North and South Uist, Mull, Easter and Wester Ross, and in Cape Breton. I have commonly seen this word translated literally as "little hatred" or "wee ugly one", given it appears to be formed from gráin ("hatred", "ugliness") and the diminutive suffix -óg 1 .
